title: Focused deferred-discussion and oral-report audit: Kedushat Shabbat and Kuntres Shvitat Shabbat

scope.description: Finite scan of the specified oral-report and deferred-discussion marker families, followed by contextual classification and focused source research. This is not an exhaustive idea-by-idea ledger and does not certify every potential parallel or inherited footnote.
scope.relationshipToPriorReview: The preceding selected-connections review is documented separately in editorial/pri-shabbos-reviewed-20261021.json. Its complete-section readings do not turn this focused marker audit into a new exhaustive subsection review.
scope.newFullContextReadingClaims: Authors read complete originating sections relevant to their assigned markers; the Shevisa author explicitly read full sections 1 and 7 and scanned all 50 Shevisa paragraphs. Independent reviewers read full origin and target paragraphs and necessary adjacent contexts as specified below, without claiming a second full reading of every section.

method.scan: Consonant-normalized scan of every preferred canonical paragraph, followed by reading the context of each broad hit. Expanded checks included שמעתי/שמענו, קבלתי/קיבלתי, deferment abbreviations, להאריך, ארוכים, במקום אחר, and self-reference wording.
method.offsets: Inventory offsets refer to the normalized scan text; they are audit locators, not reader phrase indices.
method.approvalStandard: Exact contiguous Hebrew, faithful English with editorial additions visibly bracketed, a precise source reference, enough quotation to complete the relevant thought, full target context, a separate explanation that adds value at the actual marker, and independent bilingual review.
method.attributionRule: An unnamed teacher is not identified from context alone. Explicit attribution, later explanatory parallels, and modern editorial source suggestions remain distinct.
method.rejectionRule: No fixed school quota. Weak thematic matches, circular anthology reprints, and conflicting legal formulations are not promoted as exact corroboration.
method.footnotePlacement: Forward Hebrew footnote anchors use the existing English Sources and commentary presentation. Multiple lexical markers covered by one substantive note are not counted as multiple notes. No reciprocal note is implied.

independentPeerReviews.reviewExtent: Independent second bilingual review of the four records in deferred-root-draft.json. Read complete originating paragraphs and adjacent argument, complete quoted target paragraphs, Beit Yaakov Toldot 8:1–3, Takanat HaShavin 6:1–3, and Sod Yesharim Seventh Night of Pesach 33:4–6. Every selected Hebrew excerpt was independently checked as a unique raw contiguous span of the preferred local canonical paragraph. No claim is made here to a fresh full-section reading of Kedushat Shabbat 1 and 3; the author performed that reading.

recordAssessments.exactHebrew: Unique contiguous match; the excerpt is the complete parenthetical retrospective discussion, omitting only outer parentheses.
recordAssessments.translation: Faithful. The tentative וכמדומה is retained. The first abbreviated ר״י is correctly expanded Rabbi Yochanan from Berakhot21a, and the last as Rav Yehudah from the ending of Rosh Hashanah; the translation does not silently conflate them.
recordAssessments.connection: An unusually strong self-cross-reference: the target explicitly names Kedushat Shabbat, discourse1. It explains why prayer is a serious candidate for human life's principal toil before Torah takes precedence. The note appropriately refuses to reconstruct omitted criticisms of Maharsha/Rif.
recordAssessments.placement: The selected last phrase of1:4 ends at ואין להאריך כאן. This connects the forward-looking constructive explanation to the actual deferral marker.

recordAssessments.exactHebrew: Unique contiguous selection from Toldot8:3, beginning at והענין בזה and ending after the qualification explaining Yitzchak's prayer in the field.
recordAssessments.translation: Faithful across the selected passage, including the microcosm/world correspondence, suppression of destructive inclination, prayer's constriction, and the Yitzchak exception. The spelling מדוגל בזריעה is rendered interpretively but reasonably as a characteristic of sowing; 'his distinguishing quality was sowing' would be a slightly closer optional rendering.
recordAssessments.connection: The source gives an actual mechanism for prayer as constructive human labor: self-restraint turns a person into a dwelling for the Divine Presence and repairs the world. This adds content beyond repeating 'speech means prayer.' The explanation limits its claim to the constructive reading, and retaining Yitzchak prevents the excerpt from misleadingly presenting prayer in the field as an unexplained exception.
recordAssessments.placement: The shared1:4 deferred marker and theme are defensible because this is preparation for the solution developed in the succeeding argument, not a claim to identify its unprinted objections.

recordAssessments.exactHebrew: Unique contiguous full thought corresponding to Takanat HaShavin6:1 excluding its paragraph label. No qualification is removed within the paragraph.
recordAssessments.translation: Faithful. The bracketed subject [repentance] is transparently supplied from context. The distinctions between visible death, hidden derash, and the continued life of descendants are preserved.
recordAssessments.connection: Directly corroborates the specific peshat/derash and visibility distinction of the oral teaching. The note correctly states that it does not identify the unnamed original speaker. Takanat HaShavin6:3 confirms that continued life is not yet manifest to ordinary observation and does not undermine the excerpt.
recordAssessments.placement: The anchor begins כענין ששמעתי at the actual oral-transmission marker and includes the complete transmitted argument.

recordAssessments.exactHebrew: Unique contiguous opening passage of33:5, ending at an intelligible completed explanation. The unquoted remainder further supports the distinction and supplies no omitted restriction that changes it.
recordAssessments.translation: Faithful, including the embedded Aramaic Zohar, the analogy to inanimate creation, and death as concealment at the lower level. No physical immortality visible to every observer is asserted.
recordAssessments.connection: This is a substantive later Radzin development of how the two descriptions of Yaakov can coexist, not a merely topical Yaakov quotation. Its role as a later explanatory parallel rather than identification of the oral speaker is explicit.
recordAssessments.placement: The oral marker at3:3 is the right place for this explanatory qualification.

independentPeerReviews.reviewExtent: Independent bilingual review of the seven K5–6 records: selected Hebrew and English, source references, originating paragraphs, necessary qualifications, historical attribution, and value of the connection. The author read the complete originating sections and complete target paragraphs; this review does not claim a second full reading of every originating section.

recordAssessments.assessment: The complete short Eikev II entry gives the identical verse and interpretation. The explanation preserves the distinction between enduring attachment and correction of moral faults. Its short length is appropriate because the entire primary entry is quoted.

Explicit מאיזביצא attribution is present. The English condition of repentance from love was moved before the disclosure clause to make its scope unambiguous. No condition was removed. The explanation accurately separates retrospective disclosure from present moral responsibility.

The substantial primary paragraph distinguishes divine governance from an unwilling agent's merit. English notes419 at18:4 and421 at18:6 were independently located and checked. The new translation is of the original Hebrew, not the modern annotated English edition.

The selected contiguous thought includes Sinai, Jesse, inherited desire, limitations of personal effort, and divine purification. The originating paragraph explicitly uses this distinction to explain concealment after the second tablets. The note does not claim to identify the unique intended elsewhere.

The exact correspondence and the possessive-anger explanation are both present; the distinction involving the ardor of Torah scholars remains. Removed the redundant English phrase whenever we sometimes. Direct Sefaria verification confirms the Jordan episode spans Nedarim22a:11–12 and22b:1, so the printed22b citation is retained. The unlocated Sefer Yetzirah parenthesis is expressly attributed to Tiferet Yosef and is not converted into an invented exact primary locator.

The repeated received correspondence and Bekhorot juxtaposition are exact. The continuation adds the transformation of anger through laughter and Leviathan. Its native Nedarim22a citation is defensible because the episode begins there and ends on22b.

The whole entry supplies the specific person, event, verse, Avishai analogy and Zohar support. The tentative ונראה is translated it appears. Rav Tzadok's following serpent/name interpretation is clearly distinguished from the printed Ishbitz entry. No unnamed oral transmitter is identified without evidence.

independentPeerReviews.reviewExtent: Independent second bilingual review of the one Shevisa draft, with the complete originating paragraph and complete target paragraph read directly from the preferred canonical corpus.

recordAssessments.assessment: The entire Mei HaShiloach entry is quoted and faithfully translated. The note expressly declines to use this as proof of the disputed legal conclusion or identity of the oral transmitter. Rav Tzadok’s subsequent qualifications are present in the originating paragraph and are not contradicted. The shared title and summary match the already published Mishpatim note at this exact anchor. Corrected reference spacing only.

recordAssessments.connection: Unusually strong: the same two details occur together—the absence of a daily kohen blessing and the first tanna's absence of a raised step between the two courts. The target also gives the substantive discussion recalled by the origin.
recordAssessments.placement: The selected origin begins with וכן שמעתי and includes both recalled details. This is the relevant oral-transmission marker.

recordAssessments.exactHebrew: Both selected excerpts are unique raw contiguous canonical spans. The target ends after the completed explanation of Iyar, vav, and hearing as acceptance in the heart.
recordAssessments.bilingualFidelity: Faithful across the Exodus and Sea revelations, withdrawal, borrowed initial devotion, work toward acquisition, and the connecting vav. The nested Rabbi Bunim attribution remains distinct from the surrounding unnamed holy rabbi. The English explains the Hebrew loan/asking wordplay without substituting a different argument.
recordAssessments.contextAndQualifications: The selected origin describes Sinai as acquisition relative to the Sea. Its continuation then explains repeated higher cycles of faith, sight, and acquisition. The explanation now expressly preserves that relative scope and the higher recurring cycle. The target's remainder develops Iyar's preparatory work and does not contradict the selected passage.
recordAssessments.connection: Adds a precise intermediate mechanism, rather than merely repeating the topic: Iyar joins the first gift of sight to inward acquisition in Sivan, and the loan image explains the light's withdrawal.
recordAssessments.placement: The shared origin begins at ושמעתי and preserves the Sea-to-Rephidim-to-Sinai reasoning. It properly anchors this close parallel to the oral teaching.
correctionsResolved: Explanation now explicitly preserves the relative scope of acquisition and the repeated cycle at higher levels.

recordAssessments.exactHebrew: Origin and target each match exactly once as contiguous canonical passages. The target opens with the explanatory body following the quoted Rephidim/Zohar introduction and ends with a complete account of the continuing need for prayer and service.
recordAssessments.bilingualFidelity: Faithful, including the embedded Zohar, the distinction between permitted self-examination and putting God to the test, the despair after the light disappears, and the coexistence of attachment above with necessary work below.
recordAssessments.contextAndQualifications: The remaining source paragraph explicitly returns to Amalek and the need for human clarification where it is possible; it supports the selected explanation. The note explicitly identifies this as a developed Radzin parallel rather than an identification of Rav Tzadok's oral source.
recordAssessments.connection: Explains the exact failure at Rephidim used in the origin to show that seeing was not yet acquisition: the disappearance of experienced clarity was mistaken for possible absence of the underlying bond.
recordAssessments.placement: The same ושמעתי origin span at 7:20 is appropriate. It includes Rephidim and Amalek, which this later source directly illuminates.

recordAssessments.exactHebrew: Both excerpts match their canonical paragraphs uniquely and contiguously. The target is the complete selected oral report, including consolation and eventual repair.
recordAssessments.bilingualFidelity: Faithful. The bracketed identification of the desire as the sexual desire under discussion is supported by the full target paragraph and is visibly editorial. The source's figurative biblical wording, emotional distress, consolation, and promise of repair remain in the translation.
recordAssessments.contextAndQualifications: No named identity is invented for “our holy teacher.” The explanation correctly treats the later Mei HaShiloach anthology reproduction as a locator, not an independent witness. The full source context supports the sexual-conduct antecedent.
recordAssessments.connection: Provides the indispensable consoling content alongside the rebuke: Amos 9:7 is read together with 9:9, so the quotation does not leave distressed young people with condemnation alone.
recordAssessments.placement: Anchors the first oral marker ושמעתי דפרשה זו at 7:23, addressing the report about the subject of the Amos passage. This differs from the subsequent verse-explanation marker used by the Vayigash note.

recordAssessments.exactHebrew: Both excerpts are unique raw contiguous matches. The Vayigash selection preserves the sequence of verse interpretation, the need for further exiles despite an earlier refinement, and the concluding Bar Nafli reference.
recordAssessments.bilingualFidelity: Faithful. The supplied “the reaper” is marked with brackets and is supported by the full paragraph's explicit earlier quotation; it is not passed off as a word present in the selected Hebrew span. The literal seed-drawing image, Egyptian descent, guarding against forbidden relations, seven falls, and David's fallen sukkah are retained.
recordAssessments.contextAndQualifications: The full target begins with an oral teaching about this same Amos passage. Its later continuation distinguishes Yosef's unblemished righteousness from David's work of repentance, explains that Mashiach brings a thought of repentance into the community, and explicitly says that the world is not forgiven for nothing. Following root's observation, this condition is now expressly retained in the note's explanation without changing the contiguous quote. The explanation avoids reconstructing every word of the oral source.
recordAssessments.connection: Provides the actual sequence of verse interpretations deferred at the origin: sifting without losing a soul, Yehudah and Yosef, and restoration of David's sukkah. This is distinct from the shorter Chanukah note's consoling oral report.
recordAssessments.placement: Begins at the second marker וכמו ששמעתי ביאור מקצתם ואין כאן מקומו and continues into the Kedoshim connection. The distinct intended anchor should be retained when generating the footnote.
correctionsResolved: Explanation now names the necessary repentance condition in the later continuation, including the thought of repentance and the rejection of forgiveness for nothing.
